zones.label: Column 1

Supplied page subset consulted for lexical identification, not as a substitute transcription. Data: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

lines.note: Genke is the house or family of the Genji. The scan supports G and familia without OCR's extra m; Guenjis is Japanese lineage vocabulary embedded in Portuguese.

runs.text: O ſarar, ou milhorar da infirmida-

lines.note: Genki is recovery or improvement from illness. The verb is ſarar, with long s, not farar; infirmida- continues below.
Completes infirmidade and gives genki wo uru, to regain health. The historical uru spelling is vru in the source.
Genki na or genki ni gozaru means being healthy or improved. The OCR's lagueqini is resolved as the alternative marker l followed by guẽqini; the tilde abbreviates n.
Completes being better after illness. The historical milhor spelling is preserved rather than changed to modern melhor.
Genkwa, kibishii toga, is a grave crime or severe offence. The printed qua sequence is retained in the headword.
The examples concern being dealt with or punished for a grave offence. Xoxera- continues into xoxeraruru on the next row.

runs.text: Condenar, ou ſer condenado a morte,

lines.note: Completes the Japanese passive form and glosses condemning or being condemned to death. The right-edge punctuation is a comma, leading into the alternative below.
Ou justiçado adds being executed or judicially punished. This completes the severe-penalty explanation, retaining the source's st-type.

runs.text: Entrada, ou porta do caminho por

lines.note: Genkan first means an entrance or gateway on the route to a tea gathering. The Portuguese relative clause continues below.

runs.text: onde vão ao Chanoyu. ¶ Item, Porta in-

lines.note: The route leads to chanoyu; a second sense begins an inner doorway. Chanoyu is Japanese vocabulary within the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: terior por onde ſe entra em caſa dalguem.

lines.note: Completes the inner door through which one enters someone's house. This is the second architectural sense of Guenquan.

A homonymous genkan concerns the outstanding balance in accounts. The printed Japanese begins Arauaruru cuda; the c has no clear ascender, and cuda is retained literally despite its unresolved lexical identification. The following sanyō phrase and Portuguese clarify the accounting sense; a targeted external lookup supplied no clarifying parallel.
Completes the Japanese explanation as referring to what remains in the reckoning. The gloss explicitly says the remainder of the accounts; the mark in yǔ is retained as a caron.
Genrai is something sent onward as it arrived from elsewhere. Miye kitaru supplies the Japanese paraphrase; the explanation continues below.

runs.text: aßi como veo de fora: vſaſe nas cartas, & ẽ

lines.note: The object is forwarded just as it came, a usage found in letters and conversation. The source's aßi and abbreviated ẽ are preserved.
Genrai ni makase shinji soro is the example of forwarding or offering something as received. The polite ending soro is split across the physical rows.

runs.text: Aßi como veo volo offereço, ou mando.

lines.note: Ro completes soro; the translation says I offer or send it to you just as it came. The historical object combination volo remains unchanged.
A second example says that, having received it, the speaker now presents it. The scan supports Guenrai, correcting OCR Guemiai; xinjǒ continues into itasu below.
Itasu completes shinjō itasu, to present or offer respectfully. Idem assigns the same sense as the preceding forwarding example.
Genrō is illustrated by an old and wise retainer. The initial is G, not C; the caron in both occurrences is retained.
The Portuguese describes an old or long-serving and wise retainer. This completes the predicate begun by He above.
Genson is diminution or loss, paraphrased heri and senzuru. The headword's long s and the printed Japanese forms are preserved.
The loss may concern property or goods. The terminal S. is a roman written-register label and is separated from the italic gloss.
Gantan is the first morning of the New Year, paraphrased shōgachi no ashita. The headword's n and the caron in Xǒguachino are retained.

Completes the first morning of shōgachi. On the second pass the tilde lies over or very close to the first of the two a types, so the aligned baseline manhãa is retained provisionally rather than imposing the more usual manhaã pattern. Xǒguachi is italic within the Portuguese; S. is roman.

runs.text: Este mũdo, ou vida preſente & futura.

lines.note: Gentō denotes the present and future lives or worlds. Reinspection shows a faint broken mark above e, interpreted as an abbreviation tilde: Guẽtǒ, not a silently supplied full n. The following examples spell Guentǒ, and the supplied NINJAL entry supports this identification; the damaged mark remains uncertain.
Gentō nise no ongo wo aogu tatematsuru asks reverently for protection in the two lives or worlds. Ta- begins the honorific auxiliary completed below.
Tematçuru completes tatematsuru; the Portuguese begins asking protection for this world. The source's proteição spelling is retained.
Adds the other world, then introduces gentō no tsumi wo hatasu, discharging sins associated with the two lives. Fa- continues into fatasu below.

runs.text: Pagar aqui, ou ſer castigado pollos

lines.note: Tasu completes hatasu; the Portuguese speaks of paying here or being punished for sins. The cast-type is retained without a global long-s change.

runs.text: peccados feitos neſta vida, & que bum auia

lines.note: These are sins committed in this life that one would otherwise have to pay for in the next. On reinspection the initial of bum has a closed b-like bowl, unlike the clear h of hum at c2-l003. Retain baseline bum as a possible printed error for hum; an over-inked h cannot be entirely excluded.
Completes the contrast: sins incurred here would have to be paid for in the other life. The Portuguese sentence ends on this physical line.

Gentō is redirected to kentō, severe winter, with kibishii fuyu as the Japanese paraphrase. Both o-vowels carry circumflexes; the t in abbreviated Quẽtô is poorly inked and is read from residual traces and context.
The Portuguese describes the heart or greatest severity of winter, completing the entry above rather than introducing another sense of heart.
Genxa redirects to genja, the practitioner described on the preceding page. The printed x/j variation is preserved.
Genshi means an origin or beginning, paraphrased moto hajime. The definition Principio confirms that sense.
A separate genshi denotes a profound principle or mystery. Bup. labels the Buddhist context and remains roman.

runs.text: Este mundo, ou esta vida preſente.

lines.note: Genzai is the present world or present life. The two Portuguese descriptions are alternatives within one entry.
Genzan denotes seeing someone in a visit or audience. The damaged initial is G, not the OCR C, in agreement with the examples below.
Genzan ni iru and genzan suru are alternative expressions for an audience or visit. The Portuguese infinitive is Ver, not Vor, and continues onto the next line.
Completes the gloss: seeing or deliberately meeting someone. The close form depropoſito is preserved rather than respaced to modern Portuguese.
Genzō is redirected to the preferred genzan, seeing someone. Meliùs is entirely italic; its internal OCR font breaks have been removed.
Genzō suru is the example for the preceding entry. It is a standalone Japanese expression, not a Japanese word embedded in Portuguese.
Genzoku means returning to secular life, paraphrased zoku ni kaeru. The first vowel in Zocuni is o, despite damaged printing; the Portuguese subject continues below.

The religious person becomes secular again, completing the definition of genzoku. An ink blot obscures the middle of ſecular; the surviving letters and contrast with Religioſo support this reading, not the OCR faeular.

runs.text: Peßoa conhecida de viſta, ou q̃

lines.note: Genzōnin is someone known by sight. The headword has n and a caron-bearing o; viſta is the sight word, not the OCR vißta, and q̃ remains an abbreviation.
Adds someone previously seen in another person's company. The short continuation belongs to genzōnin and reaches the lower body rule without an omitted row.

runs.text: Tẽpo, ou idade de algum Rey. Vt,

lines.note: The royal-period sense of Gueô denotes the time or age of a king. Tẽpo abbreviates tempo with a tilde over e; it is not the OCR Tãpo. The historical Gueô spelling is not normalized to the following Guiô cross-reference.
Aru micadono gueôni is the example meaning in the time of a certain sovereign. The scan reads micadono, not nicaono, and the Portuguese ends with the first part of idade.
Completes idade and specifies a king. Rey belongs wholly to the Portuguese italic gloss; the isolated roman e was an OCR font error.
The second Gueô redirects to Guiô. This is a cross-reference entry distinct from the royal-period sense immediately above.
Gueôqi redirects to Guiôqi. Both circumflex-bearing o-vowels and the q in the damaged headword are retained from the scan.
Gueôraxij redirects to Guiôraxij, preserving the historical -raxij spelling. No independent Portuguese definition is supplied here.
Gueôtai redirects to Guiôtai. The terminal period is not clearly printed, so none is added to the baseline.
Gueôxǒ redirects to Guiôxǒ. The initial G and the distinction between circumflex ô and caron ǒ are visible; OCR Cueôxǒ is corrected.

runs.text: Gueppacu. Tçuqi, xemaru. i, Tçuqino fa-

lines.note: Geppaku is paraphrased tsuki semaru and tsuki no hate. The latter phrase is divided after fa- and is completed below, where the year-end sense is made explicit.
Completes hate and identifies the end of the sequence of months as Shiwasu. Xiuaſu is a Japanese month name embedded within the Portuguese definition and remains roman as printed.
Gekikon redirects to gekon. The second vowel of Gueqicon is e, not the OCR u; the Japanese headwords are not embedded Portuguese terms.
Gekiha is paraphrased sakashima nami, opposing or rising waves. The Portuguese aleuanta- is divided here and completed on the next physical line.
These are raised waves coming against the bow of a vessel. The damaged initial d of das is included within the crop and continues aleuantadas above.
Gekyō denotes surgery or a surgeon. The source spells the Portuguese words with ç and with -rurgia/-rurgião, not the OCR -ruegia/-rurgião confusion; the headword retains caron ǒ.
Gekyōja specifically denotes the surgeon. The capital Ç has a visible lower stroke and is retained rather than modernized to Cirurgião.
Gekyo is defined as a disease of the kidneys. The printed close form derins and the comma-like terminal mark are retained; this entry lacks the long-vowel sign of the two preceding surgical terms.
Gekiran means great disorder, paraphrased sakasama ni midaruru. The adjective Grande carries over into the Portuguese nouns on the next line.
Completes the definition as disturbance or revolts. The second noun reads reuoltas, with t, not the OCR reuolias.
Gekiri is equated with ashida and kutsu and translated as wooden clogs. Tamãcos retains the printed nasal abbreviation.
Gekirin denotes the anger of a royal person. The Portuguese peſſoa has two s-elements, not l followed by long s as in OCR.

Gekirin aru or nasaruru describes a ruler becoming angry. The headword ends in n, and the apparent OCR colon at the right is not separable from the broken column rule; no terminal punctuation is supplied.
Completes the reflexive Agaſtarſe and supplies the royal subject. The spurious final roman e was caused by the damaged ending and is removed.
Gekirō again denotes opposing waves. The corrected headword has e and a caron-bearing final o; the definition ends mid-word without a secure printed hyphen.

runs.text: das por proa. ¶ Item, Permet. Pertur-

lines.note: Completes the waves coming against the bow, then introduces a metaphorical sense of disturbance. Permet. is the printed abbreviated marker, with final t rather than OCR s; Pertur- continues below.
Completes perturbação and gives shikai no gekirō wo shizumuru, calming disturbances throughout the realm. The scan supplies the missing n in Xicaino; xizzumu- continues below.

runs.text: Aquietar as perturbações do mundo. i,

lines.note: Ru completes shizumuru, followed by the Portuguese translation about quieting disturbances in the world. The final i, introduces the narrower explanation on the next line.
Specifies that world here means the empire or realm. This is a gloss continuation, not a separate entry or an omitted Japanese fragment.
Gekito is paraphrased sakashima tomogara and begins a definition of enemies. The following line specifies rebellion against a lord.
Completes the definition as those risen against their lord. The historical spelling aleuantados and the long s in ſenhor are retained.
Gekishin is a rebellious retainer, paraphrased sakashima no shinka. The Portuguese divides trai-dor at this line boundary.
Dor completes traidor, and the alternative aleuantado again expresses rebellion. The text remains a continuation of the retainer entry.
Gekwan is redirected to the preferred kakwan and paraphrased hikii kurai, low rank. The Japanese cu- at the right is continued by rai on the next line.
Completes kurai, low rank, then contrasts jōkwan and gekwan. The example reads Iǒquan, not the OCR Iǒquaſi; gue- continues below.
Quan completes gekwan. The Portuguese explicitly contrasts the highest and lowest dignity or rank, confirming the paired Japanese terms above.

runs.text: Decer, ou vir do Miyaco pera outra

lines.note: Geraku means going down or coming from Miyako to another place. Miyaco is embedded in the italic Portuguese explanation, not presented as a headword or standalone synonym.
Completes the destination as another place. The short line is a genuine body continuation with no additional hidden entry in its blank right-hand area.
Geryaku is redirected to karyaku and paraphrased shita wo ryakusu. The scan begins with G, not C; ria ends the line without a securely printed hyphen.

runs.text: O abreujar, ou deixar de tocar cer-

lines.note: Cusu completes ryakusu. The Portuguese explains abbreviation or omission and breaks cer-tas at the right margin.

runs.text: tas pancadas do cabo no tanger do tabaquinho

lines.note: Completes certas and describes omitting final strokes while playing a small Japanese drum. The instrument word is the continuous tabaquinho, not the OCR Iaba quinho.

runs.text: de Iapão, &c. ¶ Item, Sincopar a pa-

lines.note: Completes the Japanese instrument description, then introduces another sense: shortening a word at its end. The pa- fragment continues as palavra below.
Completes palavra and illustrates final shortening: Isa in place of Isabel. The Japanese metalinguistic example is roman throughout, including l; the shortened name visibly begins with a capital I.
Geretsu denotes baseness or low status; geretsu na hito gives a lowly person. The scan supports G in both forms and t followed by n in Gueretna, not the OCR m.
Mem completes homem, translating the preceding Japanese phrase as a lowly man. This continuation does not introduce another entry.
Geri is described as a bowel disease. The initial of Doença is D, not OCR C; the historical expression de camaras is retained rather than replaced by a modern diagnosis.
Gerō is defined as an inferior or lesser person. The description explicitly begins a comparison within social groups, continued below; the provisional accent in Peſſòa is retained.

runs.text: nobres, ou tambem entre gente baixa.

lines.note: The comparison applies both among nobles and among people of lower standing. This completes gerō and does not alter the separate gesu entry beneath it.
Gesu is paraphrased iyashii mono and translated here as a male or female slave. The corrected initial is G and Eſcrauo has long s, not OCR j; the lower-right Gue- is a separate catchword.
